title: Aryasura's Garland of Birth Stories — the Sanskrit text
altTitles: Garland of the Buddha's Birth Stories
textType: Buddhist narrative poetry in prose and verse
author: aryasura
attributionNote: Ascribed to the poet Āryaśūra, in the tradition a Buddhist monk of the fourth century; the work retells the former births of the Buddha as a polished kāvya, and its thirty-four stories are quoted in the Sanskrit anthologies as models of the style. GRETIL's e-text follows P. L. Vaidya's edition (Darbhanga 1959, Buddhist Sanskrit Texts 21) and was input by the Digital Sanskrit Buddhist Canon Input Project.
description: The Jātakamālā tells the Bodhisattva's former lives as a series of offerings: the elephant that gives its tusks and then breaks them off, the quail that stops a forest fire, the monkey king who makes itself a bridge across the Ganges, the king Śibi who gives his eyes and then his flesh, the prince who throws himself from a cliff, the starving tigress fed with a prince's body, the sage who gives his own body for a stag — each story in prose framed by verse, and each ending with the vow that carries the Bodhisattva toward awakening. It is both scripture of the perfections and one of the finest narrative poems in Sanskrit.
historicalContext: Āryaśūra's work was translated into Chinese, Tibetan and later into European languages, and its stories travelled into the Buddhist art and the literature of Asia; Haribhaṭṭa, Gopadatta and Kṣemendra later imitated it, and the library holds the Pali Jātaka collection whose stories it retells in classical Sanskrit.
availabilityNote: Complete as GRETIL publishes it: all thirty-four jātakas in prose and verse, 1,432 passages, streamed from GRETIL at read time, one story at a time. The file prints its own title and homage above the opening verses, and the reader drops them from the text. This is the original Sanskrit, not a translation.
